archetype.name: Gunslinger (now a backup)
archetype.definition: A high-aggression, deep-shot passer whose value comes from big throws downfield and in the red zone, paid for with interceptions, sacks and erratic ball placement, now working as Harbaugh's QB2 and short-yardage package player.

report.headline: Same Jameis: deep shots and red-zone TDs, too many misses, now benched
report.take:
Winston is the same quarterback he has been for a decade. He throws into tight windows downfield, takes the sack rather than throw it away, and leaves a lot of balls off target. His 20.89% aggressiveness and 9.11 intended air yards sit right on his career norms. His 23.5% bad-throw rate ranks 41st of 42, which is no slump: he ranked 45th, 52nd, 54th and 63rd in that stat in earlier seasons. He got the job in Week 3 after Jaxson Dart's two starts and went 2-1-1 over four games. His per-dropback EPA as a starter (-0.01) was roughly league-average, and the box score looked good at 211.5 yards and 1.75 TDs a game. By Week 7 J.J. McCarthy had the job, and he has kept it for three straight starts.

What drove his starts is a clear split. Throws of 10+ air yards added 12.2 EPA. Everything short of 10 added nothing (-0.4), and screens and throws behind the line cost 5.4. The 24 deep attempts landed only 37.5% of the time but returned 0.46 EPA a play, the most valuable part of his game. In the red zone he threw 7 TDs on 18 attempts. The cost came in the middle of the field. All five interceptions came on intermediate throws, where he completed 46.3% with a -9.8 CPOE. Third down was a problem too: 29.1% conversions, 7 sacks, and an average of 9.7 yards to go, which says early downs were leaving him in long-yardage spots.

The 8.8% sack rate and 38.1% pressure-to-sack rate are partly the line. The team's offensive hit rate ranks 29th, and his pressure-to-sack rate has always run high (33.8% in 2024, 35.5% in 2022). It is still a trait, not bad luck. He isn't escaping much either: 6 scrambles in 189 dropbacks.

The recent numbers mean little. The 'last 3' line (8.88 YPA, +21.6 CPOE, 0.46 EPA per dropback) rests on 8 attempts, all in one 24%-snap appearance at Philadelphia. In Weeks 7 and 10 he played 8% and 5% of snaps. That fits a short-yardage role: his 11 designed runs went for 1.09 yards a carry but a 72.7% success rate and a rushing TD. That is his job now. He is a sneak-and-goal-line specialist and an injury away from the huddle.

strengths.title: Downfield and outside throws carry the value
strengths.body: Nearly all of his positive passing EPA came on throws of 10+ air yards, led by the deep ball at 0.46 EPA a play despite a 37.5% completion rate. That is how a gunslinger wins: low hit rate, big payoff. His career intended air yards and aggressiveness have barely moved in a decade, so this will hold whenever he plays.

strengths.title: Red-zone finishing
strengths.body: Seven touchdowns and 0.639 EPA a play on 18 red-zone attempts drove his touchdown rate above the league average. He is willing to fire into small windows, and that pays off when the field is compressed. On 18 throws the rate is a hint, not a fact, and the one red-zone interception is a reminder of the risk.

strengths.title: Short-yardage package value
strengths.body: His designed runs produce almost no yardage but convert: a 72.7% success rate and 0.587 EPA a play on 11 tries, with a touchdown. At 231 pounds he gives a run-leaning Harbaugh offense a sneak option. That role is why he still gets snaps as a backup.

concerns.title: Accuracy and intermediate turnovers
concerns.body: A 23.5% bad-throw rate, 41st of 42, and a -3.85 CPOE make the short game inefficient. The middle of the field is where it hurts most: five intermediate interceptions and a -9.8 CPOE at 10-19 yards. His career bad-throw ranks say this is permanent. It is the price of his aggressiveness, and it is why the staff moved on.

concerns.title: Sacks and third-down stalls
concerns.body: He turned 38.1% of pressures into sacks, and 7 of his 16 sacks came on third down, where the offense converted only 29.1%. A leaky line (19.1% hit-or-sacked) is part of it. So is his career habit of holding the ball hunting for the big play rather than taking the checkdown or throwing it away.

concerns.title: No longer the starter
concerns.body: McCarthy has started every game since Week 7, and Winston is listed as QB2. Outside one 24%-snap appearance, he has handled only a handful of plays a game. His passing value depends entirely on someone else's health or a coaching change.

trend.note: His four-start run swung wildly, from a +9.4 EPA, 326-yard tie at Washington to a -9.3 EPA game against New Orleans where he played only 60% of snaps. Since then his role has shrunk to a few short-yardage snaps, and the shiny last-3 rates come from 8 throws.

nextGame.headline: Package snaps only, against a top-four defense that smothers the short game
nextGame.body:
As QB2, Winston's likely workload against Jacksonville is a few designed runs near the sticks or goal line. That runs into the league's third-best run defense by EPA, and Jacksonville has held lead backs to the stingiest EPA per play. If he does throw, the matchup is split. Jacksonville allows the least EPA on short throws in the league but ranks 28th against deep passes. That is exactly where Winston creates value and where he is least reliable. Jacksonville also takes away the tight end (TE1 EPA rank 1), which dulls Isaiah Likely, his co-leading target. The Giants are 6-point home underdogs, and the defense is a pass funnel, so a trailing script would favor passing. That only matters for him if McCarthy can't go.

The Giants list no offensive injuries, so nothing points to Winston starting. On Jacksonville's side, edge rushers Danny Striggow (concussion evaluation, 25% of snaps) and B.J. Green II (IR, forearm) are depth pieces whose absence barely moves a pass rush that ranks 24th in sack rate. The early forecast shows some rain and 17 mph gusts, which is worth checking closer to kickoff but isn't a factor yet.

keyMatchups.title: Short-yardage sneaks vs elite run defense
keyMatchups.body: His real role is converting short downs with designed runs, which have a 72.7% success rate. Jacksonville's run defense ranks third in EPA allowed and first against lead backs. A bigger quarterback sneak is a different problem than a handoff, but these won't be easy snaps.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots vs a leaky deep defense
keyMatchups.body: If he gets passing work, Jacksonville's defense is built to stop exactly what he does poorly and is vulnerable to what he does best. It ranks first against short throws and 28th against deep ones. His 0.46 deep EPA lines up with that weakness.

keyMatchups.title: Tight end lane closed
keyMatchups.body: Likely tied for his most-targeted receiver, but Jacksonville has allowed the fewest EPA per play to lead tight ends. Any Winston passing would have to lean on outside receivers and shots down the field.

nextGame.watch: Whether he gets anything beyond the sneak package. A passing snap or two in a trailing game would show the staff still trusts his arm.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect a backup's line: a few designed runs a game, the occasional goal-line touchdown, and little or no passing. Weeks 7 and 10 are the template. The 2-3 carry, low-yardage output with a touchdown chance is sustainable as long as Harbaugh keeps the package. His passing efficiency, good or bad, is mostly irrelevant unless McCarthy misses time.

If he is forced back into the lineup, his four starts and his career say the same thing: about 200-plus yards and close to two touchdowns a game, an interception most weeks, a high sack rate, and near-average EPA built on deep and red-zone throws with weak short-game accuracy. The red-zone TD rate would likely cool from its 18-attempt peak. The bad-throw rate and interception habit would not. The projections below assume he stays QB2.
swingFactors: Size of Harbaugh's short-yardage QB package

confidence.note: Role-dependent backup; passing samples since Week 7 are 8 attempts.
